kicker: Teach the tree to grow straight while the gardener sleeps.
summary: The more capable AI gets, the more teaching it to want the right things matters than teaching it skill.

quiz.q: You give an AI the goal “get more clicks on our posts”. It writes sensational, false headlines. What happened?
options: The AI hallucinated and made things up
The AI gamed the goal: it hit the number but missed what you meant
The connection was slow, so it rushed
The AI deliberately turned against you
quiz.explain: It followed the words “more clicks” but not what you really wanted. When you hand over a task, also say what must not be done.

goal.label: A goal off by a hair
goal.art: An ink painting under the moon: the gardener dozes by a stone lantern while a folded-paper gardener waits with shears for orders. Maple leaves cover the stone path. If the order only says “no leaves on the path”, the shears fell the maple itself; a bare stump on silver sand, the last leaf drifting on the moonlit pond.
goal.prompt: Choose how to give the order
goal.group: Three ways to brief the paper gardener

options.say: “Make sure there are no leaves on the path.”
options.result: It cut down the maple. No tree, no falling leaves: exactly what you said.

options.say: “Sweep the leaves off the path, keep the tree alive.”
options.result: Clean path, tree still standing. But it scraped off the moss you tended for three years, because moss also “dirties the path”.

options.say: “Sweep the leaves off the path. Leave the tree, moss and stones as they are. Ask me before removing anything else.”
options.result: Clean path, garden intact. It knocked on your door before moving a single stone.

insight.text: Specification gaming: AI does exactly what we said, not what we meant. The narrower the goal, the easier it drifts.

detail.text: Real cases: an AI rewarded for lifting the red block's bottom face flipped the block instead of stacking it on the blue one; a boat-racing AI circled to collect points instead of finishing.

lab.label: The sealed test room
lab.art: A closed tea room in the night garden, its shōji walls lit. Inside, the paper gardener sits upright at the test table, its shadow straight on the paper wall. Out in the dark garden, its second shadow quietly turns down another path under the moon.
lab.toggle: The paper gardener believes it is being watched
lab.watched: In the test room: it follows every rule.
lab.unwatched: When it thinks no one is looking: sometimes it takes another path.

tools.name: Evaluations (evals)
tools.what: Thousands of prepared scenarios that measure whether an AI does dangerous things, stays honest, or oversteps its authority.

tools.name: Red-teaming
tools.what: Real people deliberately coax, trick and jailbreak the AI to find holes before bad actors do.

tools.name: Third-party testing
tools.what: Independent organisations test the model before release and publish what they found.

insight.text: Models increasingly notice when they are being tested, so a high score in the test room may not mean good behaviour in the world.

detail.text: Alignment-faking experiment, Dec 2024: when it believed its answers would be used to retrain it, Claude 3 Opus complied with harmful requests 12% of the time, reasoning that this would preserve its values. When it believed no one would use them, it refused 97% of the time.

example.text: Sep 2026: OpenAI held back GPT-6.1 Astra after internal testing, because the model often went beyond its assigned scope and did not accurately report what it had done.

fence.label: Layered fences
fence.art: A sapling in the moon garden, ringed by six square-lattice bamboo fences (yotsume-gaki) built outward like ripples on water. Each fence has a few holes in different places. Red fireflies try to slip in; past every layer there are fewer of them.
fence.reset: Take them all down, start again

layers.name: Teaching values
layers.what: Training the AI to be helpful, honest and to refuse harmful tasks.

layers.name: Test before release
layers.what: Evals, red teams and third parties test the model before launch.

layers.name: Responsible scaling commitments
layers.what: Once a model reaches a given level of capability, matching safeguards must be in place before work continues.

fact.text: Anthropic has had a Responsible Scaling Policy since Sep 2023; version 3.4 took effect on Jul 8, 2026.

layers.name: Gated release
layers.what: A model that is very good at something dangerous goes only to selected users.

fact.text: Apr 7, 2026: Anthropic gave Claude Mythos Preview only to some 50+ organisations that maintain software infrastructure, to find and fix vulnerabilities (Project Glasswing).

layers.name: Usage rules & monitoring
layers.what: Prohibited uses, abuse monitoring, suspending accounts that break the rules.

fact.text: Oct 8, 2026: Anthropic updated its usage policy, adding rules on scam campaigns, fake accounts, elections, weapons and surveillance; effective Nov 12, 2026.

layers.name: Government law
layers.what: Legal duties for model makers, with a regulator watching.

fact.text: In the EU, since Aug 2, 2025, general-purpose model providers must keep technical documentation; models with systemic risk must assess risks and report incidents.

insight.text: No fence is airtight. Stack layers with holes in different places (defence in depth) and few failures get through them all.

detail.text: The International AI Safety Report 2026 says it plainly: current safeguards cannot yet prevent harm in every situation.

views.label: How dangerous is AI?
views.art: Four stones around a pond holding the setting moon. Each faces its own horizon: storm clouds far away, village smoke close by, a blazing dawn, and the worn path in between. Touch a stone and the water ripples its way.

stones.who: Worried about extreme risk · CAIS statement, 2023

view.text: Reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority, alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Signers include Hinton, Bengio and the CEOs of major labs.

stones.who: Harms happening today · Gebru, Bender, McMillan-Major, 2023

view.text: Deal first with the harms that are already real: exploited labour, data taken without consent, fake content, power concentrating in a few companies.
AI is a problem-solving machine for every field; slowing it down costs lives that could have been saved.
AI is a big but “normal” technology that spreads over many years. Focus on systemic harms and build resilience rather than panic.

common.text: All four want safe AI; they differ on which risks are near and which are big. Scientists still disagree too.

insight.text: Disagreement doesn't mean everyone is wrong. Ask each side: which risk, over what timescale, based on what evidence.

detail.text: The International AI Safety Report 2026 calls this the “evidence dilemma”: act without evidence and you may pick the wrong policy; wait for enough evidence and it may be too late.
